[8] Mr Vasquez did not attend the hearing of the disciplinary Charge. However, he was
represented by his counsel.
[9] At the conclusion of the liability hearing, the Tribunal indicated that the Charge and
three particulars were not established, and therefore the Charge would be dismissed.
[10] Since the hearing of the Charge, the Tribunal has also considered the applications by the
PCC and the practitioner for the respective interim non-publication orders to be made
permanent.2
[11] We set out the reasons for our decision and the orders made below.
Evidence and agreed summary of facts
[12] The parties filed an Agreed Summary of Facts (ASOF) signed by Mr Vasquez3 and an
Agreed Bundle of Documents (ABOD / Bundle).4
[13] The Bundle included the text messages from Mr Vasquez to [Ms Y] and her reply, the
complainant; an email notification from [Ms W], General Manager of [Health Centre] to the
Nursing Council confirming Mr Vasquez’s employment was terminated on Friday 7 October
2022; and the accompanying investigation letters from his employer.
[14] On the day of hearing, Mr Rusero, counsel for the practitioner, filed a statement from
Mr Vasquez.5 This statement, discussed below, included a Certificate of Achievement
confirming that Mr Vasquez had completed a Code of Conduct course with the Nursing Council
in April 2024.

[15] A letter was received from a GP at the medical centre where Mr Vasquez is a patient.6
[16] The Agreed Summary of Facts is set out below
1. On 27 February 2020 Edward Vasquez ("RN Vasquez") gained registration as
a Registered Nurse in New Zealand after completing a Bachelor of Science
nursing at Our Lady Fatima University.7
2. At the time of the conduct, RN Vasquez was employed as a registered
nurse at [Health Centre] in [location]. He had been employed in this role
since August 2022.
3. RN Vasquez’s current annual practising certificate ("APC") expires on 31
December 2024. He is currently working as a registered nurse at an aged
care facility, Presbyterian Support - Enliven, Northern branch in
Auckland.
4. [Health Centre] [location] provides comprehensive [procedure] services
to patients in the [region]. The clinic has [branches] in [location] that
service patients on the [regions].
5. [Ms Y] was a patient at [Health Centre]. At the time, she was a 21-year-
old female who was studying at university and living alone in [location].
She had been referred for a colonoscopy at [Health Centre]. A
colonoscopy is a very invasive procedure, especially for a young woman,
and often can be exposing for the patient in the recovery process. Given
[Ms Y’s] age, living situation and the nature of the procedure, she was a
patient in a vulnerable position.
6 Document 5, Letter from Henderson Medical Centre dated 7 August 2024.
7 Bundle, p 23, ASOF fn1 Edward Vasquez's registration details.
6

6. On 19 September 2022, [Ms Y] had a scheduled colonoscopy at [Health
Centre]. RN Vasquez was the nurse that admitted and provided care to [Ms
Y] in her time at [Health Centre]. He looked after [Ms Y] during her recovery.
7. RN Vasquez put in [Ms Y’s] IV line. When he removed it, it bled quite a lot
so he rebandaged it for her.
8. Shortly after [Ms Y] was discharged, she received a text from an unknown
number [contact number] at 6.23 pm which stated:
"Hey! Edward (your nurse) here! (wink emoji) Bleeding stopped? (grin emoji)
9. [Ms Y] thought that the text was a routine follow up from [Health Centre]
and believed that the text had been sent from the clinic's phone. Accordingly,
[Ms Y] responded by text:
"Yes bleeding all stopped!! Thank you so much (smile emoji)"
10. At 7.23 pm on 25 September 2022, RN Vasquez again texted [Ms Y] from his
personal phone:
"Hey! (smile emoji) how are you?" Okay if I text you? No? (cold sweat emoji)"
11. [Ms Y] felt like the second text message from RN Vasquez was "incredibly
inappropriate" and made her feel "quite uncomfortable". In her email to
[staff member] at [Health Centre] on the following day (26 September 2022)
[Ms Y] stated:
"I would expect the contact information I provided to be used by the clinic and its
staff for purposes related to my procedure and any aftercare but not this. I just
wanted to make the clinic aware of this occurrence".
7

12. [Ms Y’s] complaint was referred to the General Manager of [Health Centre],
[Ms W]. [Ms W] spoke with [Ms Y] on the phone to discuss her complaint
and followed up with an email to advise [Ms Y] about the next steps of the
investigation.
13. [Ms W] initiated an employment investigation regarding [Ms Y’s] complaint
with HR partner [name]. RN Vasquez was invited to a meeting with [Ms W]
and [HR partner] to discuss the complaint. RN Vasquez admitted that he had
texted [Ms Y] having used [Ms Y’s] admission documentation to obtain her
personal phone number. RN Vasquez admitted that he was still working at
the time that he sent the first text message and agreed that he could have
used the work phone to contact [Ms Y] when he was concerned about her
bleeding, or asked another member of the team, such as the coordinator, to
contact.
14. In respect of the second text message on 25 September, RN Vasquez stated
that he sent the text to [Ms Y] because he wanted someone to talk to and
had been reminded of [Ms Y] while watching a medical drama, Grey's
Anatomy. He explained his need to talk to someone because he had a lot of
things on his plate due to some personal issues. RN Vasquez stated that he
had not texted the patient again and that he would delete her phone number
from his personal devices.
15. On 7 October 2022, [Health Centre] terminated RN Vasquez's employment
effective immediately.
16. On 12 October 2022, [Ms W], General Manager of [sic] made a notification
to the Nursing Council of New Zealand ("the Council") regarding RN Vasquez'
conduct towards [Ms Y].
8

17. On 19 October 2022, Clare Prendergast, Deputy Registrar of the Council
referred the notification from [Ms W] to the Health and Disability
Commissioner ("HDC").
18. On 31 October 2022, HDC referred the matter back to the Council, and under
delegation from the Council, Ms Prendergast referred the matter to a
Professional Conduct Committee ("PCC") under section 65(2) of the Health
Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003.
19. On 11 August 2023, RN Vasquez and his counsel Max Rusero ("Mr Rusero")
met with the PCC in October 2023. Mr Rusero submitted to the PCC that RN
Vasquez initially texted [Ms Y] to follow up with her because she had
returned to the clinic after her colonoscopy with bleeding. The PCC noted
that there was no written documentation of this, and it was the first time the
information had been raised.
20. In another submission, Mr Rusero said to the PCC that RN Vasquez thought
it would be appropriate to text [Ms Y] because he had seen her wave to one
of the senior doctors at the clinic. The PCC were unable to draw a connection
between this submission and the text messages.
21. Mr Rusero also explained to the PCC that the reason for RN Vasquez's second
text message was because he was watching a documentary and someone
who had a similar procedure started bleeding.
22. RN Vasquez confirmed to the PCC that he was watching Grey's (sic) Anatomy
at the time and thought to text [Ms Y] the second time because he was
concerned that that bleeding could happen to her.
23. On 4 October 2023, the PCC determined to refer RN Vasquez's conduct to
the Health Practitioners Disciplinary Tribunal.
9

[17] Mr Vasquez confirmed that he admitted the facts in the ASOF and admitted that the
charge as particularised in Particulars 1.1 to 1.3 both separately and cumulatively amounts to
professional misconduct and that such conduct is of a nature that warrants the imposition of
a disciplinary sanction.
Relevant law
Burden of proof
[18] The burden of proof is on the PCC. This means that it is for the PCC to establish that the
practitioner is guilty of professional misconduct.
[19] In professional disciplinary cases, the appropriate standard of proof is the civil standard,
that is, proof to the satisfaction of the Tribunal on the balance of probabilities, rather than the
criminal standard of proof.
Professional misconduct
[20] The primary purpose of the Tribunal’s disciplinary powers is the protection of the public
by the maintenance of professional standards.
[21] Section 100 of the Act defines the grounds on which the health practitioner may be
disciplined. Mr Vasquez has been charged with professional misconduct under both
s 100(1)(a) and/or (b) of the act as follows:
100 Grounds on which health practitioner may be disciplined
(1) The Tribunal may make any 1 or more of the orders authorised
by section 101 if, after conducting a hearing on a charge laid
under section 91 against a health practitioner, it makes 1 or more
findings that—
(a) the practitioner has been guilty of professional misconduct
because of any act or omission that, in the judgment of the Tribunal,
10

amounts to malpractice or negligence in relation to the scope of
practice in respect of which the practitioner was registered at the time
that the conduct occurred; or
(b) the practitioner has been guilty of professional misconduct
because of any act or omission that, in the judgment of the Tribunal,
has brought or was likely to bring discredit to the profession that the
health practitioner practised at the time that the conduct occurred.
[22] In B v Medical Council of New Zealand8 the Court stated:
The structure of the disciplinary process set out by the Act which rely in a large part
upon judgement by a practitioner’s peers, emphasises that the best guide to what
is acceptable professional conduct is the standards applied by competent, ethical
and responsible practitioners. But the inclusion of lay representatives in the
disciplinary process and the right of appeal to this Court indicates that usual
professional practise, while significant, may not always be determinative;
reasonableness of the standards applied must ultimately be for the Court to
determine taking into account all the circumstances including not only practise but
also patient interests and community expectations including the expectation that
professional standards are not to be permitted to lag. The disciplinary process in
part is one of setting standards.
[23] The Tribunal and the Courts have considered the term “professional misconduct” under
s 100(1)(a) on many occasions. In Collie v Nursing Council of New Zealand,9 Gendall J
described negligence and malpractice as follows:
Negligence or malpractice may or may not be sufficient to constitute professional
misconduct and the guide must be standards applicable by competent, ethical and
responsible practitioners and there must be behaviour which falls seriously short of
8 Elias J, HC Auckland HC 1/96, p 15 noted at [2005] 3 NZLR 810.
9 [2000] NZAR 74 at [21].
11

that which is to be considered acceptable and not mere inadvertent error, oversight
or for that matter carelessness.
[24] Gendall J further addressed the issue and said:10
Clearly it envisages conduct in the performance of the nurse’s usual professional
duties if it amounts to “malpractice or negligence” that requires in line with
authorities an accepted view, that the negligence or malpractice be of a serious
degree and such as to be substantially below the standards expected of a nurse.
[25] “Malpractice” is defined in the Collins English Dictionary11 as:
1. Law. Improper treatment or culpable neglect of a patient by a
physician or of a client by a lawyer … 2. Gen. A criminal or illegal action:
wrongdoing, misconduct.
[26] Section 100(1)(b) of the Act creates another route by which a finding of professional
misconduct may be made. This is where the practitioner’s conduct has or is likely to bring
discredit on the particular health profession. In Collie v Nursing Council of New Zealand,
Gendall J considered the meaning of conduct likely to bring discredit on the nursing profession
as follows:12
To discredit is to bring harm to the repute or reputation of the profession.
The standard must be an objective standard with the question to be asked
by the Council being whether reasonable members of the public, informed
and with knowledge of all the factual circumstances, could reasonably
conclude that the reputation and good-standing of the nursing profession
was lowered by the behaviour of the nurse concerned.
10 At [23].
11 Collins English Dictionary (2nd Edition).
12 Collie v Nursing Council of New Zealand [2001] NZAR 74 at [28].
12

Threshold test for disciplinary sanction
[27] There is a well-established two-stage test for determining professional misconduct in
this jurisdiction.13 The two steps are:
(a) First, did the proven conduct fall short of the conduct expected of a reasonably
competent health practitioner operating in that vocational area? This requires an
objective analysis of whether the health practitioner’s acts or omissions can
reasonably be regarded as being negligence and/or malpractice or having brought
or likely to bring discredit to the practitioner’s profession; and
(b) If so, whether the departure from acceptable standards has been significant
enough to warrant a disciplinary sanction for the purposes of protecting the public
and/or maintaining professional standards?
[28] In Martin v Director of Proceedings,14 the High Court has said that the threshold should
not be regarded as “unduly high” but that “a notable departure from acceptable standards”
is required, and that threshold is to be reached with care, having regard to both the purpose
of the Act and the implications for the practitioner.
Professional standards and guidelines
[29] The Nursing Council’s Code of Conduct (2021) (the Code of Conduct) is the professional
standard for nurses that covers their conduct and provides a Code of Ethics.
[30] Principle 5 of the Code of Conduct requires that nurses must “respect health consumers’
privacy and confidentiality”. This includes, but is not limited to:
(a) Standard 5.1 “Protect the privacy of health consumers’ personal information”;
13 PCC v Nuttall 8/Med04/03P; F v Medical Practitioners Disciplinary Tribunal [2005] 3NZLR 774 (CA), as
applied in Johns v Director of Proceedings [2017] NZHC 2843 at [78].
14 [2010] NZAR 33, Courtenay J at [32].
13

(b) Standard 5.2 “Treat as confidential information gained in the course of the nurse/health
consumer relationship and use it for professional purposes only”;
(c) Standard 5.6 “Health records are stored securely and only accessed or removed for the
purpose of providing care;”
(d) Standard 5.7 “Health consumers’ personal or health information is accessed and
disclosed only as necessary for providing care”; and
(e) Standard 5.8 “Maintain health consumers’ confidentiality and privacy by not discussing
health consumers, or practice issues in public places including social media.”
[31] Principle 7 of the Code of Conduct requires that nurses to “Act with integrity to justify
health consumers’ trust”. This includes the requirement in 7.13 that nurses must:
…. maintain a professional boundary between yourself and the health
consumer and their partner and family, and other people nominated by the health
consumer involved in their care”.
Principle 8 requires that nurses must “Maintain public trust and confidence in the
nursing profession”. This includes standard 8.1 to:
Maintain a high standard of professional and personal behaviour.
Liability – Tribunal’s consideration of the Charge
PCC’s submissions
[32] Mr McClelland KC, counsel for the PCC, submitted that Mr Vaquez has, or through his
counsel, offered a number of explanations for his conduct. When considering these, it is
important to have regard to the Tribunal’s position as previously stated on many occasions
that personal reasons do not justify the unauthorised access of a client’s personal private
information, including their patient records. Mr Vasquez’s reasons include:
14

(a) He had subjective intentions to do what he believed was in the best interests of
the client.
(b) In respect of the text on 25 September, Mr Vasquez told his employer that he sent
this because he wanted someone to talk to and had been reminded of his patient
while watching a medical drama, Grey’s Anatomy.15 He said he needed to talk to
someone because he had a lot of things on his plate due to some personal issues.
(c) A further explanation offered to the PCC16 by his counsel was that he had texted
[Ms Y] to follow up with her because she had returned to the clinic after her
colonoscopy and was bleeding. Neither of these decisions was correct. There is
no evidence that [Ms Y] returned to the clinic, and it appears that the bleeding
arose from the removal of her IV line.17 The text sent was on the same day as the
surgery.18
(d) A further explanation offered by counsel19 to the PCC was that Mr Vasquez
thought it was appropriate to text [Ms Y] because he had seen her wave to one of
the senior doctors at the Clinic.20 The PCC were unable to draw a connection
between this submission and the text messages.
[33] Accordingly, Mr McClelland submitted that whether there is an explanation or
combination of explanations the Tribunal accepts, if indeed it accepts any, they do not make
Mr Vasquez’s conduct acceptable or anything other than a serious breach of accepted
standards. Counsel submitted that Mr Vasquez’s use of [Ms Y’s] private records in the terms
that he did was seriously inappropriate.

[34] The PCC submitted that given the terms of the Code of Conduct and previous decisions,
Mr Vasquez admitted his conduct amounts to malpractice and conduct that brings discredit
to the nursing profession and warrants a disciplinary sanction.
Practitioner’s submissions
[35] Mr Vasquez did not attend the hearing. He filed a statement of evidence. In Vasquez’s
statement he said:
At the time of the events occurring, I had a strong subjective view to do the best for
the client that I worked with. I went as far as defending my position that what I did
was for the best interests [sic] of the client. … I accept and apologise that my
subjective view caused me the error of judgement. I sincerely apologise for my
error of judgement that caused unfair encroachment into the client’s private space.
I wish to apologise to the client, my sister who left employment with [Health Centre]
because of the allegations, my former employer and to everyone involved that my
subjective view was wrong and caused me regrettable error of judgement.
[36] Mr Rusero, counsel for the practitioner, submitted that Mr Vasquez admitted the Charge
as set out in the ASOF.
[37] Mr Rusero submitted that there were two occasions, not three in which Mr Vasquez
sent a text message to [Ms Y].
[38] In respect of the second text message on 25 September (particular 1.3), counsel
reiterated that Mr Vasquez said he sent the text to [Ms Y] because he wanted someone to talk
to and had been reminded of [Ms Y] while watching a medical drama, Grey’s Anatomy. He
explained his need to talk to someone because he had a lot of things on his plate due to some
personal issues.
16

[39] Mr Vasquez stated that he had not texted the patient again and that he would delete
her phone number from his personal devices.21
[40] Mr Rusero submitted that there was no intention or ill will on Mr Vasquez’s part and
now Mr Vasquez has the realisation that his conduct was inappropriate, and he has apologised
for that.22 Mr Vasquez said in his statement:
I do not wish to defend the allegations, nor do I wish to appear before the Tribunal
in person. I have been stressed mentally, socially and financially since the matter
started.
[41] Mr Rusero submitted that that Mr Vasquez’s behaviour was an error of judgement.
Comparable cases
[42] Counsel for the PCC referred the Tribunal to the following cases involving unauthorised
access by nurses to patient information.
[43] In Park,23 Ms Park was an enrolled nurse (non-practising) who inappropriately accessed
the health information of a patient when she had no authority to do so and was found by the
Tribunal to be in breach of the patient’s privacy. Over a three-month period, Ms Park accessed
the health file of a patient on five separate occasions. She did so in the context of a traumatic
episode (the details of which were suppressed).
[44] In Mrs S,24 the same issue arose involving a registered nurse’s multiple (85) unauthorised
access of medical records was considered by the Tribunal. The Tribunal summarised previous
similar cases,25 and relevant legislative and Code provisions where it was noted:26

In the decisions of Paterson and Park, the Tribunal concluded that multiple breaches
of unauthorized access amounted to professional misconduct both separately and
cumulatively. As the Tribunal noted in both those instances, personal reasons for
accessing health information could not provide a justification for doing so.
[45] In Mrs L,27 the nurse was found to have accessed and viewed electronic clinical records
of her colleagues Mr and Mrs Y and the members of their family without authority to do so.
The Tribunal found that there has been a serious abuse of the privilege by the nurse when
accessing patient records other than for the proper care of patients.28
[46] In T,29 the practitioner was charged with professional misconduct with a multitude of
particulars (alleging that while employed as a registered nurse at a hospital, she
inappropriately accessed and viewed the electronic clinical records of patients not under her
care and of her colleagues and their family members, her former colleagues and their family
members, and staff. She accessed the patient files of 64 individuals which meant she had
opened well in excess of a thousand screens of information containing the health records. The
charge of professional misconduct was established.
[47] In Sheenan,30 the nurse was charged with professional misconduct in respect of his
interactions with a vulnerable mental health patient whom he had texted on many occasions
(mainly social in nature), taken her out to a café, to a restaurant and to the movies and given
her money; he also accessed her clinical records on two occasions which he had no authority
to do so. The charge was established.

Consideration of the Charge
[48] The Tribunal now turns to consider each of the three particulars of the Charge separately
and cumulatively to assess whether the PCC has established the Charge to the requisite
standard.
[49] The conduct was admitted by Mr Vasquez and there is an Agreed Summary of Facts.
Nonetheless, it remains for the Tribunal to make its own assessment of the evidence and
whether the conduct amounts to professional misconduct warranting a disciplinary sanction.
Particular 1.1 – Accessing her confidential details from her patient file to contact [Ms Y] on his
personal phone
[50] [Ms Y] had a scheduled colonoscopy at the [Health Centre] on 19 September 2022. Mr
Vasquez was the nurse that admitted and provided care to [Ms Y] during her time there. He
looked after her during her recovery.
[51] Mr Vasquez put in [Ms Y’s] IV line. When he removed it, it bled quite a lot so he
rebandaged it for her.31
[52] Shortly after [Ms Y] was discharged, she received a text from Mr Vasquez at 6.23pm. Mr
Vasquez has admitted that he accessed [Ms Y’s] private records to get in touch with her to
check whether the bleeding had continued.
[53] The Tribunal considers that it was appropriate for Mr Vasquez, as [Ms Y’s] nurse to access
her details and follow up in a professional capacity. However, he should not have used his
personal phone for this purpose.
[54] The Tribunal also recognises that while it is not best practice, it is not unusual for a
registered nurse to use their private phone to contact a patient for work related matters.
31 Agreed Summary of Facts at [6] and [7].
19

[55] During the employment, investigation Mr Vasquez admitted that as he was still working
on 19 September at the time that the first message was sent, and that he could have used the
work phone to contact the patient or asked another member of the team such as the Co-
ordinator to contact the patient.32
[56] The Tribunal observes that at the time of this incident, Mr Vasquez was in the early
stages of his employment with [Health Centre], having commenced work in early August 2022.
[57] The Tribunal is not aware of what policies were in place for the use of work or personal
phones. Nor was it provided with the hospital’s policy on personal cell phone use, which may
or may not have been part of Mr Vasquez’s orientation to the workplace.
[58] The Tribunal finds on the balance of probabilities that Mr Vasquez’s access to [Ms Y’s]
personal details was not a breach of privacy or a breach of Standard 5.6 of the Code of
Conduct. Mr Vasquez’s access to [Ms Y’s] personal information could reasonably be
considered as part of his duty of care to follow up with his patient.
[59] While the Tribunal accepts that it would have been preferable to use the work phone,
Mr Vasquez honestly disclosed that he used his personal phone.
[60] The Tribunal is not satisfied on the balance of probabilities that particular 1.1 is
established as negligence or malpractice in Mr Vasquez’s scope of practice.
[61] Particular 1.1 is not established as negligence or malpractice in Mr Vasquez’s scope of
practice or conduct that has brought discredit to the nursing profession.

[69] As set out above, the Tribunal accepts that in the context of patient care where Mr
Vasquez had rebandaged the IV line, this text message may reasonably be regarded as
following up with his patient in the course of his work.
[70] [Ms Y] has also indicated that in terms of receiving a message, she was comfortable
with this initial contact albeit that the text message had an emoji. She thought that this was a
routine follow-up message and did not express concern about this message.
[71] The Tribunal is not satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, that particular 1.2 is
established as negligence or malpractice in Mr Vasquez’s scope of practice. Nor is it satisfied
that the contact made by Mr Vasquez in this first text was a breach of [Ms Y’s] privacy under
Standard 5 of the Code of Conduct.
[72] Particular 1.2 is not established as negligence or malpractice in Mr Vasquez’s scope of
practice or conduct that brings discredit to the nursing profession.
Particular 1.3 – On 25 September 2022 at 7.23pm six days later, Mr Vasquez texted [Ms Y]
again with the message “Hey! (smile emoji) how are you?” “Okay if I text you? No? (cold sweat
emoji)”
[73] The second text was sent six days following the procedure at the Clinic and out of hours.
This text could be viewed in various ways and [Ms Y] felt uncomfortable. This is of concern to
the Tribunal.
[74] By comparison with the first text message (particular 1.2), [Ms Y] was concerned that
the text message was sent six days later and was personal in nature. She took the step of
notifying her concerns to [Health Centre]. [Ms Y] stated:
However last night (25 September) I received another message from that phone
number asking “Hey! how are you?” “Okay if I text you? No?”
I felt this was incredibly inappropriate and made me feel quite uncomfortable. I
would expect the contact information I provided to be used by the Clinic and its
22

staff for purposes related to my procedure and any aftercare but not this. I just
wanted to make the Clinic aware of this occurrence.
[75] The Tribunal also accepts that the text and use of emojis is unprofessional in this context
and can have many meanings.
[76] Sending a text message with the cold sweat emoji is regarded as a nervous emoji. For
example, it can mean “I am very nervous, so I am just going to keep smiling. You can use this
sweat emoji when you feel nervous laughter bubbling up in your chest.”34
[77] Another source suggests that the cold sweat emoji means “Intended to depict nerves or
discomfort. It is commonly used to express a close call as if saying ‘Phew’ and wiping sweat
from the forehead”.35
[78] Overall, the use of these emojis suggest that Mr Vasquez was tentative in his inquiry.
Whilst he might have had an ulterior motive that could infer a breach of professional
boundaries with a patient, there was no follow up to the text.
[79] Mr Vasquez’s nervousness was reflected in the wide-ranging explanations he gave the
PCC.
[80] Mr McClelland did not however, go so far as to suggest that there were sexual overtones,
rather, that Mr Vasquez has accessed the patient’s private information. He then used [Ms Y’s]
information through his personal phone by texting her using emoji interspersed with the text
message in an inappropriate manner.36
[81] In the Tribunal’s objective assessment of the evidence, although the second text
message was inappropriate, this was a one-off situation and not repetitive.

[82] The Tribunal accepts Mr Rusero’s submission, and as stated by Mr Vasquez, he made an
error of judgement. Mr Vasquez used a patient’s private information to make contact with her
outside of providing clinical care. While this was in breach of Standard 5.6 for accessing
personal information, the Tribunal is not satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, that this
was conduct which falls seriously short of acceptable standards expected of a nurse.37
[83] Particular 1.3 is not established as negligence or malpractice in Mr Vasquez’s scope of
practice or conduct that has brought discredit to the nursing profession.
Liability findings
[84] The Tribunal is not satisfied that each of the three particulars of the Charge, either
separately or cumulatively, establish negligence or malpractice in Mr Vasquez’s scope of
practice.
[85] Nor does the Tribunal consider that separately or cumulatively Mr Vasquez’s conduct as
set out in the three particulars is conduct that brings discredit to the nursing profession.
[86] [Ms Y] accepted that the first text message soon after her visit to the clinic was
appropriate and then rightly questioned the second text received some days later. The
Tribunal has concluded that while this behaviour from Mr Vasquez was inappropriate, it is not
conduct to such a serious degree that reflects poorly on the nursing profession.
[87] Therefore, it is not necessary for the Tribunal to undertake the second step of
assessment and apply the disciplinary threshold.
[88] In the alternative, and if the Tribunal is wrong about its assessment, it considers that the
inappropriate conduct at its highest - the second text message (particular 1.3) – is a one-off
incident and does not demonstrate a pattern or course of conduct which raises any concerns
about the practitioner’s risk to the public that would warrant a disciplinary sanction.
37 Collie at {21] and [23].
24

[89] The circumstances of this case are clearly distinguishable on the facts from the cases
referred to by the PCC above.38 In those cases, there were often repeated breaches of patient
privacy involving unjustified access to patients’ records. In this case, the Tribunal finds that
the initial contact by Mr Vasquez to [Ms Y] was justified, although his subsequent contact with
[Ms Y] was not satisfactory given that the subsequent text was six days after [Ms Y] visit to the
Clinic.
[90] Not all breaches of professional standards amount to negligence or conduct that
warrants a disciplinary sanction. For example, in PCC v H,39 where it was alleged that among
other aspects of the Charge, a paediatric nurse practised outside her scope of practice in
administering intravenous Propofol, Fentanyl and Ketamine without a prescription and failed
to follow the appropriate policy relating to verbal orders for medications.
[91] In PCC v H,40 the Tribunal found that the established particulars and sub-particulars
cumulatively amounted to a falling short of the conduct expected of a reasonably competent
nurse. However, the Tribunal was not satisfied that the gravity of the conduct in the
circumstances of this case warranted disciplinary sanction and no penalty was imposed.
[92] The Tribunal is not satisfied that the gravity of the conduct in the circumstances of this
case warrants disciplinary sanctions for the purposes of protection of the public and
monitoring professional standards. To impose a penalty on this practitioner would be a
disproportionate response to the seriousness of the conduct in question.
[93] The Tribunal has no concerns regarding protection of the public. Mr Vasquez has
demonstrated some insight into his actions by apologising and accepting full responsibility. He
has attended a Code of Conduct education seminar held by the Nursing Council.
[94] Accordingly, the one Charge of professional misconduct, including three particulars is
dismissed.

Application for permanent name suppression
[95] Both the PCC and Mr Vasquez applied to make permanent interim non-publication
orders under s 95 of the Act.41
[96] Following the hearing, the Tribunal issued timetabling directions and subsequently
considered the respective applications by the PCC and the practitioner for the interim non-
publication orders to be made permanent. 42
Principles
[97] There are well settled legal principles that apply when the Tribunal considers an
application to suppress the name of any person and/or identifying details appearing before
the Tribunal.
[98] These applications are made pursuant to s 95 of the Act. Section 95 provides as follows:
95. Hearings to be in public unless Tribunal orders otherwise
(1) Every hearing of the Tribunal must be held in public unless the Tribunal
orders otherwise under this section or unless section 97 applies.
(2) If, after having regard to the interests of any person (including without
limitation, the privacy of the complainant) and to the public interests, the
Tribunal is satisfied that it is desirable to do so, it may (on application by any
of the parties or on its own initiative) make any 1 or more of the following
orders:
…….
41 Interim non publication Orders were made by consent pursuant to s 92A of the Act for the practitioner on
26 July 2024 and the PCC witnesses on 7 August 2024 prior to and for the duration.of the hearing.
42 Minute of the Tribunal in relation to applications for permanent name suppression dated 17 September
2024.
26

(d) An order prohibiting the publication of the name, or any particulars of the
affairs of any person.
[99] The starting point in any consideration of name suppression is the fundamental principle
of open justice, as set out in s 95(1) of the Act: there is a presumption that the Tribunal’s
hearings will be held in public unless the Tribunal orders otherwise.
[100] The principle of open justice and the underlying rationale of transparency of court
proceedings to maintain public confidence in the administration of justice has been endorsed
by the Supreme Court.43
[101] The public interest factors to be considered by the Tribunal have been identified in a
number of decisions. These include:44
(a) Openness, transparency and accountability of the disciplinary process;
(b) Protection of the public;
(c) Maintenance of professional standards;
(d) Public interest in knowing the identity of a health practitioner charged with a
disciplinary offence;
(e) Importance of freedom of speech and the rights enshrined in s 14 of the New
Zealand Bill of Rights Act;
(f) Unfairly impugning other practitioners’ reputations being affected by suspicion.
[102] In relation to the maintenance of professional standards, the Court of Appeal noted in
Y v Attorney-General,45 that in disciplinary proceedings, the public interest and open justice
43 Erceg v Erceg [2016] NZSC 135 at [2].
44 [2020] NZHC 2828 Edwards J at [40].
45 [2016] NZCA 474 at [32].
27

generally favour the publication of names of practitioners facing disciplinary charges, so that
existing and prospective clients – patients – can make informed choices, The Court said in this
context:
Consequently, a professional person facing a disciplinary charge is likely to find it difficult to
advance anything that displaces the presumption in favour of disclosure.
[103] Section 95(2) gives the Tribunal discretion to consider whether to suppress the name of
any person appearing before the Tribunal where the Tribunal is satisfied that it is desirable to
make such an order, taking into account the privacy interests of any persons (the practitioner
and other parties) and the public interest.
[104] The threshold test of what is “desirable” in the disciplinary jurisdiction does not require
exceptionality and invokes a considerably lower threshold than the usual civil test.46 It
requires the Tribunal being “satisfied that it is desirable to do so”. This requires the Tribunal
to make an evaluation of competing considerations of the interests of any person and the
public interest against the starting point of open justice.47
[105] A useful summary of these competing considerations was provided by the Court in
Anderson v PCC,48 where Gendall J said:
[36] Private interests will include the health interests of a practitioner, matters that
may affect a family and their wellbeing, and rehabilitation. Correspondingly,
interest such as protection of the public, maintenance of professional standards,
both openness and “transparency” and accountability of the disciplinary process,
the basic value of freedom to receive and impart information, the public interest in
knowing the identity of a practitioner found guilty of professional misconduct, the
risk of other doctors’ reputations being affected by suspicion, are all factors to be
weighed on the scales.
46 Johns v Director of Proceedings [2017] NZHC 2843, Moore J at [166].
47 Ibid at [166]-[167].
48 HC, Wellington, CIV 2008-485-1646 (14 November 2008).
28

Practitioner’s application
[106] The practitioner provided an affidavit in support of his application for permanent name
suppression.49
[107] The PCC indicated it would abide the decision of the Tribunal.
[108] No new information was submitted by Mr Rusero in support of the application to make
the interim order permanent. In summary, three grounds can be inferred.
[109] Firstly, the shame and the humiliation that Mr Vasquez has brought to his sister who left
her employment in New Zealand for Australia, noting that his sister may return because the
humiliation has settled.
[110] Secondly, Mr Vasquez stated that it is now one year and 10 months since he was
dismissed from his employment with [Health Centre].
[111] Mr Vasquez provided a letter from his GP indicating that he had received treatment for
anxiety in November 2023. He applied for name suppression so that he can continue to
recover.
Analysis
[112] It is well established that where a charge of professional misconduct is proven, the
practitioner will be named in the preponderance of cases. What may be considered
“desirable” at the time of an interim application for non-publication may be considered
differently after a substantive hearing when an adverse finding is made.50
[113] Conversely, it does not necessarily follow that permanent name suppression should be
granted where a Charge has been dismissed.
49 Affidavit of E C M Vasquez dated 2 August 2024.
50 T v Director of Proceedings Panckhurst J HC Christchurch, CIV-2005-409-2244, 24 February 2006 at [42]
cited in Johns v Director of Proceedings [2017] NZHC 2843 per Moore J at [166].
29

[114] In Director of Proceedings v Merilos,51 the charge of professional misconduct was
dismissed following a defended hearing where it was alleged that a nurse had slapped a
patient when he was working in a rest home.
[115] In respect of the application for permanent name suppression, the Tribunal recognised
that often, following the dismissal of a charge, there will be a compelling case which would
satisfy it that a permanent order should be made, but in that case, it was not so satisfied. The
Tribunal applied a number of factors including financial and reputational prejudice and in the
circumstances of the case discharged, the interim order of the practitioner’s name and made
permanent the non-publication of others involved in the incident, and the institution.
[116] Similarly, in Spence, 52 the Tribunal found the practitioner not guilty of the charge but
declined permanent name suppression.
[117] In the present case, the Tribunal is not satisfied that it is desirable for a permanent non-
publication order of the practitioner’s name and identifying details to be made. This is for the
following reasons.
[118] Firstly, the Tribunal considers the open justice principles are very important and should
be given considerable weight in this case. There is public interest in the Tribunal having a
transparent process for disciplinary proceedings.
[119] Secondly, although at the interim stage the Tribunal was satisfied it should make an
order having regard to an unresolved charge and that the circumstances that Mr Vasquez left
his employment, the situation has now changed. The practitioner will now be able to disclose
that the Charge was dismissed and there is no finding of professional misconduct.
51 Director of Proceedings v Merilos Nur08/11D.
52 930/HP17/392P. The PCC appealed the Tribunal’s decision and the practitioner appealed the decision
declining permanent name suppression but withdrew that appeal following the overturning of the
Tribunal’s not guilty decision on appeal.
30

[120] The permanent non-publication order of the PCC witnesses and the employer and
institution set out below will mitigate the public information surrounding the circumstances
of the Charge.
[121] Thirdly, while the Tribunal accepts that it is nearly two years since Mr Vasquez was
dismissed from his employment, there is no evidence of financial prejudice as the Tribunal
was advised that he is working as a nurse in a rest home.
[122] Fourthly, the Tribunal also recognises that there is a degree of reputational prejudice for
Mr Vasquez, and it has affected his health, but in the circumstances of this case it is not
satisfied that there is sufficient evidence regarding these private factors that would outweigh
the important open justice factors.
[123] The application for a permanent non-publication order of the practitioner’s name and
identifying details is declined.
PCC’s application
[124] Counsel for the PCC filed an application for a permanent non-publication order of the
names and identifying details of the following PCC’s witnesses and clinic.
[Ms Y]
[Ms W]
[Ms A]
[Mr S]
[Health Centre]
[125] Mr Rusero, counsel for the practitioner consented to the PCC’s application for a
permanent non-publication order.
31

[126] [Ms Y] is the complainant in this case. The Tribunal is satisfied that it is desirable that
her name and the associated staff at [Health Centre], including the name of the institution
and identifying details should not be disclosed in this decision.
[127] The PCC’s application to make the interim non-publication order of PCC witnesses
permanent is granted.
Result
[128] Accordingly, the Tribunal dismisses the one Charge of professional misconduct.

details is discharged; and
